why: Wikipedia and Oxford Learner's both define a gelding as a castrated (male) horse.
Wikipedia (Sheep) and Cambridge define a wether as a castrated male sheep.
Wikipedia and the FishBase glossary (mouth brooder = oral brooder) describe fish (and Darwin's frog) holding eggs/young in the mouth.
Wikipedia and Stanford Birds describe the cuckoo laying in other species' nests as brood parasitism.
Wikipedia and Stanford Birds: precocial chicks hatch downy with open eyes, leave the nest early and feed themselves; chickens and ducks are examples.
German Wikipedia and DWDS both give 'Feuerqualle' as the colloquial name of Cyanea capillata.
NOAA and Wikipedia name Physalia physalis the Portuguese man o' war, a siphonophore with a sail-like float.
Wikipedia and the US standard of identity (27 CFR 5.147) define rum as distilled from sugar-cane juice, syrup or molasses.
Wikipedia, Cambridge and Oxford: Calvados is a Normandy brandy made from (cider) apples, with pears allowed; answer right.
Guinness World Records holds the fastest-growing-plant record for certain bamboos at up to 91 cm per day; Wikipedia agrees.
Guinness and Wikipedia: Hyperion, a coast redwood in Redwood National Park, is the tallest living tree (115.55 m in 2006, ~116 m now).
Guinness and Wikipedia: the parasitic Rafflesia arnoldii has the largest single flower (~1 m, up to 11 kg).

The Gymnosperm Database calls the White Mountains bristlecone 'Methuselah' officially the oldest tree; an unconfirmed older (~5,067 y) tree is the same species, and only clonal organisms (Old Tjikko, Pando) are older, which the body already says.
BBC (2008) and Wikipedia: Old Tjikko, a Norway spruce with ~9,550-year-old roots, stands in Dalarna, Sweden.

Wikipedia calls giant bamboos the largest members of the grass family (culms to 46 m); Guinness gives giant bamboo up to 50 m. No second source spells out 'tallest grass' in so many words, hence medium.
Australian Museum and Wikipedia: the red kangaroo is the largest living marsupial (males up to ~90 kg; AM says 92 kg).
Australian Museum, Tasmanian government (NRE) and Wikipedia: the world's largest surviving carnivorous marsupial, now only in Tasmania.
Tasmanian government: the thylacine was the largest marsupial carnivore since Thylacoleo, and the last known one died in Hobart Zoo on 7 September 1936; Wikipedia agrees.
Australian Museum and Wikipedia: a threatened wombat dives into its burrow and uses its tough rump to block or crush the attacker.
Wikipedia and Cambridge define mutualism as an interaction where both species benefit; DWDS supports the German answer 'Symbiose' in its everyday sense.

answer: Salad cucumbers are grown in greenhouses, ridge cucumbers in the open field
why: RHS: greenhouse varieties vs outdoor (ridge) cucumbers; German Wikipedia: Salatgurken are grown almost only under glass, and field-grown ones are sold as Landgurke.

answer: White asparagus grows under mounded soil without light, green asparagus above ground in the light
why: Penn State Extension: keeping light off emerging spears gives white asparagus; Wikipedia: the spears are earthed up and cut below the soil.

answer: Winter wheat is sown in autumn, spring wheat in spring
why: USDA ERS and Wikipedia: winter wheat is sown in the fall, spring wheat in spring.

answer: Wet rice grows in flooded paddies, upland rice on dry fields
why: Wikipedia: upland (dry) rice grows on rain-fed dry land, not in flooded paddies; the second source is an old corpus quotation (DWDS, 1924) making the same contrast. No agronomy agency page could be fetched (IRRI/FAO/Ricepedia URLs dead), hence medium.

answer: Arabica grows in the highlands, Robusta in the lowlands
why: The National Coffee Association's table: arabica at higher altitudes, robusta at lower altitudes; Wikipedia gives arabica's usual 1,200–1,500 m.

FishBase: pilot fish accompany sharks and eat their parasites and scraps. FishBase calls this commensal, so the card's 'because' is the popular explanation, but the answer stands; the article note already names remoras as an arguable alternative.
Scientific American, Australian Museum and Wikipedia: holometaboly is complete metamorphosis with a pupal stage (beetles, butterflies...).
Same three sources: hemimetaboly is incomplete metamorphosis without a pupa (grasshoppers, true bugs).
Cambridge and Wikipedia: a cocoon is the silk casing a caterpillar pupates in.
Monarch Joint Venture, the National Wildlife Federation and Wikipedia: the newly hatched larva eats its eggshell (chorion) before starting on milkweed.

Mongabay (from the Reptile Database): Australia 1,145 reptile species, ahead of Mexico 1,015 and Brazil 868; live Reptile Database queries give 1,168 vs 1,029.
FAO FRA 2020 Key findings lists the Russian Federation first among the top five forest countries (815 Mha chart); Wikipedia says Russia has more forest than any other country.
